speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, I want to thank you, and I want to thank the folks here at Case Western Reserve for hosting this tonight. It’s a very important event, and they’ve done a superb job of putting it together.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, you have 90 seconds to respond.

speaker: Edwards
text: Thank you.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 30 seconds to respond, Mr. Vice President.

speaker: Cheney
text: We’ve made significant progress in Iraq. We’ve stood up a new government that’s been in power now only 90 days. The notion of additional troops is talked about frequently, but the point of success in Iraq will be reached when we have turned governance over to the Iraqi people; they have been able to establish a democratic government. They’re well on their way to doing that. They will have free elections next January for the first time in history.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 30 seconds, Senator.

speaker: Ifill
text: Time for a new question but the same topic. And this time to you, Senator Edwards.

speaker: Edwards
text: Here’s what it means: It means that Saddam Hussein needed to be confronted. John Kerry and I have consistently said that. That’s why we voted for the resolution. But it also means it needed to be done the right way.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, you have 90 seconds to respond.

speaker: Cheney
text: The senator has got his facts wrong. I have not suggested there’s a connection between Iraq and 9/11, but there’s clearly an established Iraqi track record with terror.

speaker: Ifill
text: You will respond to that topic, but first I want to ask you for two minutes, Vice President Cheney.

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, we’ve never let up on Osama bin Laden from day one. We’ve actively and aggressively pursued him. We’ve captured or killed thousands of Al Qaida in various places around the world and especially in Afghanistan. We’ll continue to very aggressively pursue him, and I’m confident eventually we’ll get him.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, you have 90 seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: Someone did get it wrong. But it wasn’t John Kerry and John Edwards. They got it wrong. When we had Osama bin Laden cornered, they left the job to the Afghan warlords. They then diverted their attention from the very people who attacked us, who were at the center of the war on terror, and so Osama bin Laden is still at large. Now, I want to go back to something the vice president said just a minute ago, because these distortions are continuing.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, 30 seconds.

speaker: Cheney
text: Twenty years ago we had a similar situation in El Salvador. We had — guerrilla insurgency controlled roughly a third of the country, 75,000 people dead, and we held free elections. I was there as an observer on behalf of the Congress.

speaker: Edwards
text: The vice president just said that we should focus on state sponsors of terrorism. Iran has moved forward with its nuclear weapons program. They’re more dangerous today than they were four years ago.

speaker: Ifill
text: New question to you, Senator Edwards, but I don’t want to let go of the global test question first, because…

speaker: Ifill
text: … I want people to understand exactly what it is, as you said, that Senator Kerry did say.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, let me say, first, he said in the same segment — I don’t remember precisely where it was connected with what you just read — but he said, point blank, “We will never give anyone a veto over the security of the United States of America.”

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, you have 90 seconds to respond.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, Gwen, the 90 percent figure is just dead wrong. When you include the Iraqi security forces that have suffered casualties, as well as the allies, they’ve taken almost 50 percent of the casualties in operations in Iraq, which leaves the U.S. with 50 percent, not 90 percent.

speaker: Edwards
text: May I respond briefly?

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, you have 30 seconds.

speaker: Cheney
text: Your rhetoric, Senator, would be a lot more credible if there was a record to back it up. There isn’t. And you cannot use “talk tough” during the course of a 90-minute debate in a presidential campaign to obscure a 30-year record in the United States Senate and, prior to that by John Kerry, who has consistently come down on the wrong side of all the major defense issues that he’s faced as a public official.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, a new question for you. You have two minutes to respond.

speaker: Cheney
text: I’m saying specifically that I don’t believe he has the qualities we need in a commander in chief because I don’t think, based on his record, that he would pursue the kind of aggressive policies that need to be pursued if we’re going to defeat these terrorists. We need to battle them overseas so we don’t have to battle them here at home.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, you have 90 seconds to respond.

speaker: Edwards
text: Thank you.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, you have 30 seconds.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, Gwen, I think the record speaks for itself. These are two individuals who have been for the war when the headlines were good and against it when their poll ratings were bad.

speaker: Ifill
text: And 30 seconds…

speaker: Edwards
text: John Kerry has been absolutely clear and consistent from the beginning that we must stay focused on the people who attacked us; that Saddam Hussein was a threat that needed to be addressed directly; that the weapons inspectors needed to have time to do their job.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, new question to you, and you have two minutes to respond.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, let’s start with what we know. What we know is that the president and the vice president have not done the work to build the coalition that we need — dramatically different than the first Gulf War. We know that they haven’t done it, and we know they can’t do it.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, you have 90 seconds.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, Gwen, it’s hard to know where to start; there are so many inaccuracies there.

speaker: Edwards
text: Thank you.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President?

speaker: Cheney
text: Classic example. He won’t count the sacrifice and the contribution of Iraqi allies. It’s their country. They’re in the fight. They’re increasingly the ones out there putting their necks on the line to take back their country from the terrorists and the old regime elements that are still left. They’re doing a superb job. And for you to demean their sacrifices strikes me as…

speaker: Edwards
text: Oh, I’m not…

speaker: Cheney
text: … as beyond…

speaker: Edwards
text: I’m not demeaning…

speaker: Cheney
text: It is indeed. You suggested…

speaker: Edwards
text: No, sir, I did not…

speaker: Cheney
text: … somehow they shouldn’t count, because you want to be able to say that the Americans are taking 90 percent of the sacrifice. You cannot succeed in this effort if you’re not willing to recognize the enormous contribution the Iraqis are increasingly making to their own future.

speaker: Ifill
text: New question, similar topic, because I want to circle back to a question which I’m not quite certain we got an answer to.

speaker: Ifill
text: It’s a question of American intelligence.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, let me speak, first of all, to what the vice president just said, and then I’ll answer that question.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President? CHENEY: Gwen, the story that appeared today about this report is one I asked for. I ask an awful lot of questions as part of my job as vice president. A CIA spokesman was quoted in that story as saying they had not yet reached the bottom line and there is still debate over this question of the relationship between Zarqawi and Saddam Hussein.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, in June of 2000 when you were still CEO of Halliburton, you said that U.S. businesses should be allowed to do business with Iran because, quote, “Unilateral sanctions almost never work.”

speaker: Cheney
text: No, I do not. And, Gwen, at the time, I was talking specifically about this question of unilateral sanctions.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards?

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, the vice president talks about there being a member, or someone associated with Al Qaida, in Iraq. There are 60 countries who have members of Al Qaida in them.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President?

speaker: Cheney
text: I can respond, Gwen, but it’s going to take more than 30 seconds.

speaker: Ifill
text: Well, that’s all you’ve got.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, the reason they keep mentioning Halliburton is because they’re trying to throw up a smokescreen. They know the charges are false.

speaker: Ifill
text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: These are the facts.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, as we wrap up the foreign policy part of this, I do want to talk to you about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, first of all, I do agree that we’ve been largely absent, not entirely absent, but largely absent from the peace-making process over the last four years.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, 90 seconds.

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, I want to go back to the last comment, and then I’ll come back to Israel-Palestine.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, it’s your turn to use 30 seconds for a complicated response…

speaker: Edwards
text: That was a complete distortion of my record. I know that won’t come as a shock.

speaker: Ifill
text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: Cheney
text: Oh, I think his record speaks for itself. And frankly, it’s not very distinguished.

speaker: Ifill
text: In that case, we’ll move on to domestic matters. And this question, I believe, goes to Senator — to Vice President Cheney.

speaker: Cheney
text: I think it goes to Senator Edwards.

speaker: Ifill
text: It goes to the Senator. I see you. I just asked him about Israel, even though we didn’t actually talk about it much.

speaker: Cheney
text: I concede the point.

speaker: Edwards
text: No, I did talk about it, Israel. He’s the one who didn’t talk about it.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, the Census Bureau ranked Cleveland as the biggest poor city in the country, 31 percent jobless rate.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, Gwen, there are several things that I think need to be done and are being done.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, you have 90 seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: Gwen, your question was about jobs?

speaker: Ifill
text: It was about jobs, and it was about poverty.

speaker: Edwards
text: I thought it was about jobs and poverty. I hope we get a chance to talk about education, but that’s what the vice president talked about.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President?

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, we’ve got 111 million American taxpayers that have benefited from our income tax cuts.

speaker: Ifill
text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: The vice president and president like to talk about their experience on the campaign trail. Millions of people have lost their jobs. Millions have fallen into poverty. Family incomes are down, while the cost of everything is going up.

speaker: Ifill
text: This next question goes to you, Senator Edwards.

speaker: Edwards
text: Because we will do what they’ve not done. You know, if you look at what’s happened over the last four years, we have gone from a $5 trillion projected surplus when George Bush took office to a $3 trillion projected deficit.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 90 seconds, Mr. Vice President.

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, the Kerry record on taxes is one basically of voting for a large number of tax increases — 98 times in the United States Senate.

speaker: Ifill
text: Thirty seconds, Senator Edwards.

speaker: Edwards
text: We are committed to cutting back anything in our programs that need to be cut back to get us back on a path to fiscal responsibility.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 30 seconds, Mr. Vice President.

speaker: Cheney
text: Yesterday, the president signed an extension of middle- class tax cuts, the 10 percent bracket, the marriage penalty relief and the increase in the child tax credit.

speaker: Ifill
text: The next question goes to you, Mr. Vice President.

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, you’re right, four years ago in this debate, the subject came up. And I said then and I believe today that freedom does mean freedom for everybody. People ought to be free to choose any arrangement they want. It’s really no one else’s business.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, 90 seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: Yes. Let me say first, on an issue that the vice president said in his last answer before we got to this question, talking about tax policy, the country needs to know that under what they have put in place and want to put in place, a millionaire sitting by their swimming pool, collecting their statements to see how much money they’re making, make their money from dividends, pays a lower tax rate than the men and women who are receiving paychecks for serving on the ground in Iraq.

speaker: Ifill
text: New question, but same subject.

speaker: Edwards
text: No. I think we’ve both said the same thing all along.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, you have 90 seconds.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, Gwen, let me simply thank the senator for the kind words he said about my family and our daughter. I appreciate that very much.

speaker: Ifill
text: That’s it?

speaker: Cheney
text: That’s it.

speaker: Ifill
text: OK, then we’ll move on to the next question.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, Gwen…

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President?

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards?

speaker: Edwards
text: Yes. Well let me say, first of all, I’m proud of the work I did on behalf of kids and families against big insurance companies, big drug companies and big HMOs.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, new question to you, same topic. Do you feel personally attacked when Vice President Cheney talks about liability reform and tort reform and the president talks about having a trial lawyer on the ticket?

speaker: Edwards
text: Am I personally attacked?

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President?

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, we think lawsuit abuse is a serious problem in this country. We think we badly need tort reform.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 30 seconds to respond.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, first of all, I have paid all the taxes that I owe.

speaker: Ifill
text: Thirty seconds, Mr. Vice President.

speaker: Cheney
text: We’ve done a lot to reduce the cost of health care. The Medicare drug benefit that we’ll be providing to seniors beginning in ’06 will provide upwards to $1,300 a year to help them buy prescription drugs.

speaker: Ifill
text: I will talk to you about health care, Mr. Vice President. You have two minutes. But in particular, I want to talk to you about AIDS, and not about AIDS in China or Africa, but AIDS right here in this country, where black women between the ages of 25 and 44 are 13 times more likely to die of the disease than their counterparts.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, this is a great tragedy, Gwen, when you think about the enormous cost here in the United States and around the world of the AIDS epidemic — pandemic, really. Millions of lives lost, millions more infected and facing a very bleak future.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, you have 90 seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, first, with respect to what’s happening in Africa and Russia and in other places around the world, the vice president spoke about the $15 billion for AIDS. John Kerry and I believe that needs to be doubled.

speaker: Ifill
text: OK, we’ll move on.

speaker: Edwards
text: The American people want in their president and in their vice president basically three things: They want to know that their president and their vice president will keep them safe. They want to know that they have good judgment. And they want to know that you’ll tell them the truth.

speaker: Cheney
text: You want me to answer a question about his qualifications?

speaker: Ifill
text: That was the question.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 30 seconds, if you’d like to respond to that.

speaker: Edwards
text: I think the most important thing I’ve learned from this process is what I now know about John Kerry. I knew him before. I know him better now.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, I clearly believe that George W. Bush would be a better commander in chief. He’s already done it for four years.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, picking up on that, you both just sang the praises of the tops of your ticket.

speaker: Cheney
text: Why I am different from John Edwards. Well, in some respects, I think, probably there are more similarities than there are differences in our personal story.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, you have 90 seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: Mr. Vice President, we were attacked. But we weren’t attacked by Saddam Hussein. And one thing that John Kerry and I would agree with you about is that it is…

speaker: Ifill
text: You just used John Kerry’s name.

speaker: Edwards
text: Oh, I’m sorry. I broke the rule.

speaker: Ifill
text: Would you like to respond? Thirty seconds.

speaker: Ifill
text: OK, we’ll move on. This goes to Senator Edwards.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, first of all, let me say that John Kerry has — I can use his name now?

speaker: Edwards
text: OK. John Kerry has been, as have I, been completely consistent about Iraq. We’ve made very clear from the beginning — and not an afterthought; we said it at the time — that we had to confront Saddam Hussein and that we had to have a coalition and a plan to be successful.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President? CHENEY: Well, Gwen, I can think of a lot of words to describe Senator Kerry’s position on Iraq; “consistent” is not one of them.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 30 seconds if you choose.

speaker: Edwards
text: Yes, but they didn’t fund the mandates that they put on the schools all over this country. That’s the reason 800 teachers — one of the reasons — 800 teachers have been laid off, right here in Cleveland. One-third of our public schools are failing under this administration. Half of African-Americans are dropping out of high school. Half of Hispanic-American are dropping out of high school.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President?

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, No Child Left Behind, they were for it; now they’re against it. They voted for it; now they’re opposed to it.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, our final — I’m sorry, you have 30 seconds, Senator Edwards.

speaker: Edwards
text: Are you sure — yes, he started. Yes, 30 seconds, please, yes.

speaker: Ifill
text: I did figure out I was wrong.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, in fairness, if you feel like you need to go to him, we’ll — I’ll stop. IFILL: Well, I do, because we’re actually on the final question. I apologize for giving you an extra 15 seconds there. I go now to Vice President Cheney.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, I must say it’s one of the disappointments of the last four years, is that we’ve not been able to do what the president did in Texas, for example, when he was able to reach across the aisle and bring Democrats along on major issues of the day.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator, there’s 90 seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: Thank you.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 30 seconds to respond to that, Mr. Vice President.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, Gwen — I’m sorry, it’s hard to know where to start.

speaker: Ifill
text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: They had a choice on allowing prescription drugs into this country from Canada, of being with the American people or with the drug companies. They were with the drug companies.

speaker: Ifill
text: As previously agreed, we’ll go to closing statements now, two minutes each.

speaker: Edwards
text: Thank you.

speaker: Ifill
text: Vice President Cheney?

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, I want to thank you.

speaker: Ifill
text: And with that, we come to the end of tonight’s debate.
